blocks.x: Okay, tape is rolling.
Uh, let's see. This is Rio One of Nick Plytus, am I getting it right? Dead right. Uh, and we're in Seminar Room Two of the Howard Tilton Library, Tulane University.
What's today's date, October the what?
Eight. Eight. Eight, 1963 it is. Ah, the first question. When you were born and where? I always like to know that so I can get some sort of...
Ah, yes, I was born in Melbourne, Australia. Um, July 1927.
July. No date, just July. Ah, second July. Second July, I see. 1927. And, uh, you've come here, you've been on a tour, huh?
Yes. Um, we took a band to England. Uh, we had a contract for six months. And, uh, managed to get the extensions of it and, uh, quite a few months in Germany. So we lasted nearly two years. Ah.
And that's just finished. And that's just finished. When did you finish?
That finished in April. In April, I see.
And you've been travelling round and about since? I've been having a holiday. Well, now, uh, how did you get interested in playing music?

Just from listening to records, uh, when I was very young. Uh, just preferred to listen to, uh, to music than go out and play with the gang. Um, got onto, uh, a few jazz records after a few false starts and, uh, that was it.
You didn't play an instrument then?
No, no.
Did nobody in your family play?
No.
What was the very first thing that got you started? Uh, was it a record or a movie or a single live band or what?

Um, I saw the movie Birth of the Blues, um, when it first came out. I didn't know anything about the music, but I liked it. And, uh, particularly the, uh, the, uh, long black instrument that seemed to tie up all the loose ends and keep things rolling. Uh, that's supposed to be a description of a clarinet. Um, but it was from listening to records, uh, really. Um, then I met a few chaps there who were going through the same, uh, sort of stage. We got together and tried to play.
Uh, who was the clarinet playing with then?
Uh, Danny Parlow.
How did you find that out, Danny?
I found it out later. Uh, hmm. Yes, I didn't know at the time. Uh, hmm.
I just wondered about the clarinet. Yes, well, um...

I guess it was Teagarden's band. It was Teagarden's band, yes. I looked it up particularly because I was interested. I remembered that, uh, that was the first time I could have heard any jazz and, uh, appreciated it.
Well, you found other friends who were interested in that.

Yes. There was, um, just at that time, uh, Graham Bell was starting to, uh, get a few jobs and play around, uh, at a few dances. And, uh, this would be the early forties. Um, he, his brother Roger, Ade Monsborough, and, uh, a clarinet player called Pixie Roberts, were the, the first, uh, first line, I'd say, of, uh, Australian jazz. It was in Melbourne, Australia, that it all, uh, seemed to get going. Um, Graham organized his band after the war, and, uh, they did a trip to Czechoslovakia to a world youth festival. Um, yeah. They went on to England, started the first English Jazz Club, I believe. Um, but by the time they came back to Australia, um, quite a few other bands had, uh, got going. Um, and there was quite, quite a bit of interest in, in jazz for a while. I suppose next, uh, to Graham Bell's band would, uh, come the Southern Jazz Group from, uh, Adelaide, South Australia, run by Dave Delwitz, who played trombone. Um, with a very, um, very fine trumpeter, Bill Munro, and, uh, Bruce Gray, an excellent clarinetist. Um. Um. Um. They were the...
How did they sound, uh, the, uh, Southern Jazz Group and Graham Bell? Are they... would you think that they had any particular model, or...?

Well, the, the Graham Bell band, uh, was styled more on the Lou Waters type than anything else, with the peculiarly Australian sound, uh, I always think. It might be Roger Bell's trumpet, that's the quarter there. Um. Um. The... Southern Jazz Group were, were less, uh, less stilted, I'd say. Um. Had a wonderful, uh, tuba player, Bob Wright. Very, uh, very good player.

I still, when I listen to them, I think, you know, of this King Oliver, and, uh, I think, uh, King Oliver influence, coming down through waters and all that. Yes. When I, what a little I've heard of them, you know. Mm. They're still in that general framework, huh?
Yes, yes. Mm-hmm.
And what about, uh, was Tony Newstead going at that time?

Tony Newstead was playing about, he never seemed to, sort of, uh, get a band and keep it for any length of time. He was, uh, uh, you'd call on a Chicago kick. Um. Mm-hmm. Like, to play, uh, a bit like Bix. Um. It was looser stuff, in many ways, um, happier, sort of easygoing stuff. He was a very nice player. Mm-hmm. Uh, but he was never a, sort of a, a force as a band leader. The bands were Graham Bell and the Southern Jazz Group, followed by Frank Johnson and Lynn Bernard. They're about the four bands as such. Yeah.
Well, what did Frank Johnson and Lynn Bernard play?

What approach did they turn? They were, uh, much looser. Um. Um. Still on a type of what is kick, but not, uh, not so much. Um. Len Bernard, uh, that, that was the Frank Johnson band. Len Bernard was, um, um, Louis Armstrong, Hot Five, Hot Seven band. Mm-hmm. Um. Um. And, uh, Len's young brother Bob on, uh, Cornet was, uh, really, uh, sounded much like, uh, early Louis. Too much, I suppose, but, uh, still it was nice to hear. Mm-hmm. Um. Um. Later, they, uh, they changed, brought in Ade Monsperum, uh, on alto, uh, dropped the trombone and, and played, uh, they made, uh, some very fine records, probably the best Australian, uh, records ever made. Um.
This is Len Bernard.
Len Bernard, yes. Um, I'll get a copy and send it to you.
Oh, I'd like to hear it.
Um. Ah, I can't describe that sound. It's a, a sort of, uh, a hot Clarence Williams type of, uh, sound. Mm-hmm. And it was, uh, good while it lasted. They didn't keep it up for long.
Well, the Dees bands, uh, have many original tunes, like, uh, well, the Aztec Prentice is one I think of. You remember that?
I don't know that one.
I think, uh, I think Roger Bell wrote that one.
Oh, um, yes, he wrote a few. Yeah. Um, Dave Dalwitz, uh, wrote, uh, quite a number, um, some strange ones, uh, Crocodile Creep.
Mm-hmm. That's one.

Uh, trying to get an Australian, uh, flavour into them. Um, Frank Johnson wrote a few. One that comes to mind is, uh, Hilarity Match, which was, uh, quite good in the match type of, uh, thing. Um. Um.
So you'd see the, the influence of the people you're talking about now, the Waters and, and the Johnny Dodds, and they were big over there, huh? Uh, yes.
Yes. Yes. It was all, uh, actually it was all based on, on records and, uh, it was based on those records.
And this is in the forties mostly you're talking about?

Um, into the fifties too. Um. Um. No one, uh, took, uh, any great heed of the, um, Bunk Johnson, George Lewis, uh, type of band when it came out, um, until, um, 1957 when the Melbourne New Orleans Band, uh, started. Um. Um. They stayed very much in the old, uh, mold of, uh, King Oliver Lou Bottas, sort of thing.
Well, uh, back to Frank Johnson. Who was the star of that band? Was Johnson himself a star? I know.

Was it a star? Um, no, it was, uh, it was a, uh, a good all-round band. That was the, uh, basis of it. And, uh, it was a great band to play with. Um. I remember the first time I, I played with them, uh, I became, uh, 50% better player straight away because, uh, everyone played so well, it was so easy to fit in with them. Um. They, uh, when they started, their star was, uh, just a big star. And then, uh, there was, uh, Jeff Kitchen, a clarinet player. Mm-hm. And after he left, um, Warwick Dyer, the trombone player, grew in statue, and, uh, very nice player. Unfortunately killed in an automobile accident. Um, but, uh, the Frank Johnson band was, uh, its, uh, strength was that it was, uh, playing as a band, and, uh, its ensemble work was its forte. Mm-hm. I see.
Well, uh, was Frank Johnson the first band you played with, or you played with Elie Wilhoff?
Uh, the first recognized band. I, I played, played about with anyone and everyone, uh, wherever I could. Um.
Um, on what instruments?
Well, I started on, on saxophone, but dropped that, uh, after a few years, uh, and decided the clarinet was, uh, a better instrument, and, uh, the clarinet I was, uh, tried to play.
Uh, what age were you when you took up saxophone?

Well, I bought me a saxophone when I was fifteen. Mm-hm. Just used to, uh, blow about on it. I never had lessons, which was a bad thing. It took so much longer to, uh, get anywhere. Um, I was eighteen, I suppose, when I took up, uh, clarinet.
Mm-hm.

It was always just very much of a secondary type of hobby. Mm-hm. And, uh, there's nothing, uh, there's no great musical scene in Australia to, uh, make it worthwhile financially to, uh, try and, uh, break into anything.
Well, what does the public do when they listen, then?

They dance. They dance. They don't even listen. They dance. Um, most of them are, like most publics, uh, are not very interested at all. Mm-hm. They dance to it. Which is, uh, good, I think, from the playing point of view. You can just, uh, concentrate on your playing without having to, uh, feel that you've got to move, uh, an audience that's just sitting still in front of you by doing something, uh, spectacular. So do I.

Yeah. It's a pleasant change to hear a band like that again. Very rare that you get to hear that around New Orleans anymore. Mm-hm. Dance halls are pretty well gone. There's a couple left that are still going, the Harmony Inn and the Legends, but I don't know if the bands are any good. It's a new Legends, a cousin of the old family. Anyway, uh, do they allow drinking in the jazz clubs, or do you have bars, or is it like you doing at all? No, no, no. It's, uh, it's much worse. It's ridiculous.
Uh, at six o'clock, the bars close, 6 p.m. Mm-hm. And, uh, no drink is allowed to be consumed after that time anywhere, much less in dance halls.
Uh-hm.
Um, so that, uh, it's just got to be coffee and coke, I'm afraid.
You mean that if you get drunk, you have to get drunk? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

before six at night? Yes, unless you bring your own beer and you have to drink that on the sly secretly, you're not allowed to drink it in that hall, nor within, I think, half a mile of a public dance hall. So that even if you slip round the back somewhere, if you're found, you're fine. Nothing can be more ridiculous. Yeah. That's very strange, you know. Well,

all these laws about drinking seem so strange after you've been in New Orleans. Yes. Well, you can get a drink any time of the day, unless there's an election, and you can only get beer here. You're not supposed to be too drunk when you vote here. I see. The effect in Australia

is that at 6pm the town is full of drunks because they knock off work at about 4.30 or 5 and rush to that bar to drink as much as they can in that hour on an empty stomach, and so they're a nice old mess at 6 o'clock. And when do your dances start? About 8.30 until midnight. But
it's not the all-night rave kind of thing that they have anyway? No, no, no, no, nothing like

that in Australia. Never had an all-night rave. Yeah. And what about the jazz conventions? That's an exceptional thing. It's an amateur sort of organisation done by musicians. Once a year, between Christmas and New Year for a week, they meet in one town in Australia. They travel, they travel a thousand miles, some of them. They all get together and every day and night for that week, they play and talk and drink together and have a marvellous time. It's really a wonderful experience. I've been to most of them since they began in 1946, but I can't distinguish one from another very much and I don't drink it. But you just get, well, you're just about five feet up off the floor, just playing music, talking music, having a marvellous time. It's, strangely enough, they make money. Although they're very loosely organised and there's no pretension about the presentation at all. They've become well known and they get big crowds there, make a lot of money, which is spent for good purposes, helping jazz in different ways. Well, what about the two clarinet business? Do they still do that a lot in Australia? Do you still use two clarinet much? No, not as a rule. Although if a clarinetist turns up somewhere where another band is playing, they're bound to do a two clarinet set or something like that, a couple of numbers at least. But what brings that to mind? Well, I don't know. Well, Eight Monsborough made some records, you know, the two

clarinet blues. Yes, yes. And it seems to sell that jazz group, but sometimes they had what, Tom Pickering on clarinet. He's a Tasmanian. Yeah, but I don't know why. But it seems to me that that's one of the things about the clarinet blues. Yes, they used to do it quite a bit more. Yes, they used to do it quite a bit. And of course, you have so much doubling of instruments down there. Like, well,

eight Monsborough is a classic example. Yes. It is really exceptional. It's just that he appears on so many records, I think, that might give you that impression. There isn't really very much doubling, except when eight does it. What all has he played since you've known him? What instruments? Oh, well, every instrument. Every instrument. He's quit the alto. He's changed to tenor. And plays that very well, as he plays most instruments. He was first known as Plunk Monsborough. He used to play banjo. As I say, he's played all instruments. And what kind of tenor does he play now? What style? It reminds me of, say, mid-thirties, Coleman Hawkins breathing through ballads sort of thing. Very nice, subtle sort of stuff. Most Australian stuff is a bit, I suppose, not very, not very deep. And, Aid is an exception. He's, he's a more subtle player. Most of us just aren't, probably, good enough to, to do much more than, blow out a fairly loud noise.
We didn't really get on with Warwick Dyer. He, he doubles him. Do you play piano?

Yes, um, a sort of limited but very, um, knocked out piano. Yes. Um, he was good to play with, uh, when he was playing piano because he, uh, he, uh, definitely regarded the piano as a, a tuneful drum. And, uh, beat out the chords, uh, strongly, which was great. He was, um, he was a very, um, very good, uh, trombone player, a very, uh, very hot trombone player.
Mm-hmm. Uh, did he die when he was with the Frank Johnson band?

Yes, um, we were coming back from a job, um, about a hundred miles, uh, north of Melbourne. And, uh, oh, well, it was, uh, we'd been playing at a ball. It was about three in the morning. Uh, rushing to get back, uh, rushing to get back in time to have about an hour's sleep before we went back to our jobs and, uh, going a bit too fast. Frank Johnson was driving. He ran out of the road. And, uh, uh, we, uh, went over the side, uh, all of us got injured in some way or another, but, uh, Bokka was unfortunate enough to be killed. He didn't know anything, he didn't know it to some day. Mm-hmm. Um, I got a broken neck out of him. It's still a bit gone. Um, seems to do the thing, though, musicians are always, uh, uh, a great risk because they're not going to be a bad guy. It's a great risk because they're always travelling, uh, late at night or early in the morning, and, uh, when they're all, uh, keyed up after playing music and having a few drinks and all that.
Well, what about that band? Did it continue on the Frank Johnson band?

It, uh, did continue, um, using, uh, quite a good trombone player, Frank Traynor, uh, on trombone. But, um, by this time, um, Frank Johnson's, uh, uh, idea was, uh, changing. He was, uh, under the bad influence, unfortunately, of, uh, Louis Armstrong. He was one of the first, uh, jazzmen we heard in, uh, in the flesh in Australia. Um, he started to, uh, try and play, um, in a more modern style. Um, not modern jazz, but in a mainstream sort of style. Um, which, uh, didn't suit a lot of us. Um, so that, uh, uh, by the end of 1956, I resigned. Although the band was, uh, getting a lot of work, it was, uh, not playing the same sort of music and, uh, wasn't very satisfactory. Um, so quite a few of us, uh, resigned. He got another band of, uh, rather smart players, uh, good technical players, but they, uh, they didn't have any body, really, in their playing. And, uh, breakups, you know.
What about Armstrong coming over there? Do you think that he was doing much improvising or the band was doing much improvising?

Uh, no, that, that's the trouble. They were playing, uh, showcase stuff. Um, I don't blame them. They've got to live. They've played their jazz. But, uh, they did have this bad effect on, uh, a lot of the local boys. Um, um, Um, and, uh, Armstrong just seemed to play the same, uh, tunes, the same solos. And, uh, I'm afraid, uh, a lot of the, uh, local boys just tried to do the same sort of thing, which was pretty ridiculous.

How did, uh, the, uh, whatchamacallit, uh, the, uh, the whole band, with the piano player and the trombone player and all the rest of them do the same thing? Or would some of them get off a little more?

In the Armstrong band? Yeah. Yes, um, Edmund Hall was the only one who was, uh, doing much, uh, in the front line. Billy Kyle, uh, uh, would vary it a bit, but not much. They had their set numbers and their set way of playing them and they played them. It was, uh, they were a great crowd pleaser and, uh, drew a lot of, uh, huge audience.
Showbears.
Yes, I'm afraid so.
That kind of thing.
It's, uh, it's a pity, especially with a fellow like them. It's a pity.
No. Yeah. Well, uh, so then when you left Frank Johnson, did you go immediately to another band or?

No, I thought that, uh, oh, well, no one's, uh, playing much, uh, worthwhile jazz now, so, uh, that's it. And, uh, um, I just didn't think that, uh, it'd be worth, uh, playing. Um, but a few months later, um, uh, a chap from England, uh, a trombone player called Lou Hurd, um, told me that, uh, he wanted to try and start a band. And, um, so collected a few chaps. They're not very good players, but, uh, were very keen. And, uh, it's the old story. Um, technique doesn't matter that much. And stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff Lyn Dutton, the agent in England, heard some of these records and offered us this contract in 1961. So we went over to England and that's where we've been since then.
Did your repertoire change when you went into this Melbourne New Orleans jazz band much?

Oh yes, yes, yes. Most of the tunes were new to me actually. They were based on, mainly on the records, Bunk Johnson, George Lewis and those men made, whereas previously I'd been playing King Oliver, Lou Watter's sort of tunes.
What were some of the typical ones you were playing before the Melbourne band?
Well, Lou Watter's tunes like, I think of a tune, Friendless Blues. Oh gosh.
Well anyway, what have you been playing lately with the Melbourne jazz band?

Just for contrast, I'm trying to get in on it. Yes, with the Melbourne jazz band, sometimes my burden is so hard to bear, Lord, Lord, Lord, you've been so good to me. The ones that have been played and recorded over and over again by George Lewis and others. With we hope a slightly fresh touch and trying not to be a slavish copy at all. What can I say on a George Lewis kit, just trying to play in a looser sort of style than the old Lou Watter's King Oliver type, but not to just copy records, which doesn't make sense to my mind.
What did you still have some of the, uh, I can't think of the name of that guy.
Will Johnny Dodds and the Waters clarinet players in your playing, do you feel that? Or has that influence gone out of your playing?

I never had a great Johnny Dodds influence in my playing, although I admired his playing very much. I just didn't think that it was worthwhile somehow trying to copy him. I heard a lot of chaps who did and got pretty good copies and they sounded a bit corny somehow always. I think Dodds had a bit of fire that others just couldn't copy even if they copied note for note what he played. So my playing was never a Dodds style, it was certainly not a Bob Helms style, I think he was the one, wasn't he, with Lou Wonders?
He was one of the ones and there was another one who I like even better than I do Helms and I can't think of his name. Yes, I know who you mean.
He was a rather... Holm? Yeah, Alice Holm. That's right, that's right. That's the one I'm trying to... A little more disciplined. Helm I couldn't take, I thought he got out of tune just
much too much altogether. Too wild. Too wild.

Yes. But my style changed quite a lot and I was very much criticised by the old gang as a sort of traitor. My style's been influenced, it's a bit too much like George Lewis I suppose at present, but I'll get over it I think. Well, before that you don't really have a model, huh? Oh, they always used to say I was more like Homer Simeon. I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. It's sort of a... It's sort of a... a lot of... It's a bit too much like George Lewis I suppose at present, but I'll get over it I think.
Well, before that you don't really have a model, huh?
Oh, they always used to say I was more like Homer Simeon. I don't... I don't know. Sort of a long term with a lot of people is a very interesting question.
Yeah, you mean not just on the tourist. No, I mean to people who are interested in music.
Yes, in jazz. Because he's not a clever player. He's not... Is this going over? Yeah, go ahead.
You're not a showman. You're trapped. You're not going to play this to George I hope.

No, no. I regard him as an amateur and his... That's why he's... That's why he's good. Yes. That's why also he's made a lot of records where he's out of tune and having a lot of trouble. There is one I just couldn't play it. It was so far... He was sort of... He was playing quite a good intonation himself, but he was out of tune with everyone else in the band so much that they just... He was in tune with himself, but not with anybody else.
He was in tune with himself, but not with anybody else. He was in tune with himself, yes. And this was just bad.
It sounded to me as though he was just playing and not listening to the others, which... No, maybe it was recorded under circumstances where he couldn't hear himself.
Yes, yes.
Hear the rest of the band.
They're engineers who love to do things like that.
Either that or perhaps he had a trumpet, the bell of the trumpet in his ear. That has affected me at times. I'll just hear a big echo and don't count it in.

Well, we never did put our names on here. Not Paul Crawford. You were saying your ear is stocked up. This can affect you playing, things like that. And I'm Dick Allen is my name. Put your name on that, Paul.
I coughed my name onto the tape.

Yeah. Well, I couldn't understand that cough. But... Oh, yeah. I think that's what I do, Nick Paulitis, October the 8th, 1963. Okay, now that we've got it going. But there's so many things that can affect the way a musician plays. We were talking, though, about... You say you didn't figure that it was a Simeon influence, in particular, that you went through a stage where you listened to a lot of people, obviously, from what I can judge...

Yes, I listened to a lot of jazz. I've always regarded myself as a chap interested in listening to jazz. And much more secondary and attempted player. And that's just sort of come along as the years went along. And... Really, my interest is in jazz and much less in sort of attempting to be a great player of jazz.

Well, what about the English trad scene? I mean, as you say, you feel you're very much under the influence of George Lewis. What about the bands over there? Do you feel that they are too imitative? Or that they are going to derive something from this and build it into their own? Are they commercial? Or can you generalise? Or what?

Well, just generally speaking, they came under the George Lewis influence very much some years ago. And quite a few good bands were formed. Some of them were much too imitative. But there were some quite good jazz bands formed. Unfortunately, the jazz scene grew there. And it's become very much commercialised now. There's big money to be made by some bands. Chris Barber showed that first. Followed by Ackerbilk, Kenny Ball. Their jazz content has declined rapidly as they've become popular bands. And unfortunately, that has a big effect on the other bands, the sort of secondary bands, who are also trying to cash in on this. And it's a sorry scene in England now, compared with a few years ago when there were quite a few idealist sort of players still about. But there are still some semi-professional bands who try to play jazz because they like it. Ken Collier is the first one that comes to mind. He still manages to do quite well playing full-time professionally without bowing to all the gimmicks and tricks that the others have to bow to. But other bands. Kid Martin's Ragtime Band, led by Barry Martin, who spent some time here, is a very good band. A chap called Mike Daniels. He has a very nice band. He's had it for ten years. But will not turn professional because he wants to play as he likes. And they've got a fine band. They play Jelly Roll Morton, King Oliver tunes and things like that. But in their own way, they're a good band and a different sort of band. A very happy band. Very impressive. Unfortunately, most of the bands in England are not developing at all in a good way. They're going backwards, getting onto the tradie pops kick.
And is that hitting Australia?

I've been away from Australia for two years. I'm told that it is. They've had visits from Acker Bilk and from Kenny Bull. And let me say, this Acker Bilk is still playing quite a bit of jazz and much superior stuff to Kenny Bull. But I'm told that there has been a bit of a trad movement that's grown since I left Australia. Of all people, Graham Bell, a sort of pioneer, has got in on it with a band of people who play what I would term slick Dixie. I don't know what effect this is having on the sort of secondary bands there. I hope it's not having too much of an effect on them. But the movement's so much smaller in Australia that there is more chance that the bands will stick to playing their way and not let themselves be ruled by the market too much. Mainly because there's not much of an Acker. So that it's not worth it.
What did you think of New Orleans? For example, you saw the Onward Brass Band yesterday. How did that strike you?

There were a few fleeting little seconds in which I heard them playing these little takes or a commercial that they were doing, a commercial film. It was a nice sound. I'd love to hear them marching along and playing for some length of time.
It sounded great. Was it what you expected to find a New Orleans brass band playing for a television commercial?

It's much as I expected to hear, except that I was a little worried. I did hear the Young Tuxedo Band record and it was a bit wild. This little bit that I heard of the Onward Brass Band was much more disciplined and more in tune. It had a fine sort of body and the sound was great. As for the other music I've heard, mainly at Preservation Hall, it's of great interest to me to hear these men, men that I've heard a little bit of on records, I've read a bit about, others that I hadn't even heard of. It's great to listen to them and put them into perspective and revalue them or put values on them. At the same time I'm sure it's a great help to myself, just getting an idea of what it's all about. It's very difficult just working off records. I'm sure we don't hear the full story at all on records.
How did you like meeting Raymond Burke? Describe that for Paul.

Raymond Burke is, I hadn't heard him at all. I just heard that he's supposed to be the best white clarinet player in New Orleans. I met him yesterday and he said, I don't play much in front of public. I'm a bit afraid to. They all play too fast. I'm out of practice. I don't know what it is. If you think it's because I don't play very much these days that I find it hard to keep up with it. Well I answered what seemed to be logical. Naturally I suppose if you're out of practice you're going to find it hard to just pick up a clarinet and play. You have to warm up. You have to sort of practice a bit each day if possible. It seems so ridiculous that I should be telling Ray Burke all about it. It's amazing that a chap, I've heard a bit of his stuff since. He plays a beautiful clarinet. I like it very much. He plays with a really beautiful tone. He's a subtle sort of player. It seems amazing that a chap who can play such beautiful music should even be asking questions like this. Particularly of me. It's quite a joke.

I told him. Well what do you think about the personality of the men you've met in general in New Orleans? Have you met them a little bit and talked to them? Yes. Do you find them to be braggarts or do you find them to be modest or is there any rule or what?

Modesty has been the keynote that I've found. I haven't struck one of these loud mouths. I spoke to Barney Bigard when he was in Australia with Louis Armstrong in 1954 and I was very disappointed. stuff with stuff with stuff stuff with stuff stuff with stuff

I got away from him as quickly as possible. His stuff was strictly for kids. It was ridiculous. On the other hand, a couple of years later, when the Armstrong Band came out, Edmund Hall played with them. He was a far better player and a very nice chap, who was a very kindly sort of fellow, very patient with our many questions, and really answered honestly and sincerely. Very nice chap. And that's the sort of fellow I found here so far, the chaps I've met.

It was so funny meeting Jim Robinson on the street. We were walking over to Kid Howard's house. And Jim had just stopped by Willie Parker's house. And what did he play? I'm alone because I love you. The Willie Parker. Because he walked out of the street after finishing playing with the Onward Brass pad. Then we met him. And so what did he play? About four bars of You Tell Me Your Dreams. He was just gradually drinking his way home.

Beautiful. It was marvellous. It reminds me of the sort of people we get sometimes in the audience in Australia, who have quite a few drinks and come up and say, play some Irish songs. That sort of thing.
You said he's been playing I'm Alone Because I Love You frequently at the Hall.

Yes, yes. They're playing it all the time. Sweet Emma sings it. It's fine. Jim generally starts playing it when they come in. He's obviously having a bit of a I'm Alone Because I Love You fetish or something at present.
Moonlight and Roses it was before that, when he had a few drinks he played Moonlight Roses. It's great really.
This is a kind of nabala.
Yeah.

It's very, very natural the way he plays. Jim Robinson, to my mind, plays just as well if not better now every night than as on records he made 20 years ago. It's great. He's been one of the highlights listening. Percy Humphries, I'm very impressed with Percy as a fellow who just plays the music very, very naturally as it occurs to him. Some nights he blows out, other nights he plays very casually but always very, very nicely.
Well, you were saying he impressed the crowd last night with certain ways of playing. Yes.

We talked about that earlier. Just standing up, putting a very tight mute in the trumpet playing very, very softly. Very straight really, just playing the melody. But just beautifully, nice subtlety. And that brought the house down more than all the loud when the saints sort of stuff. No clowning or anything. Just very, very quiet. In fact, obviously it's a great, it's a great old lesson there. Make the audience listen. Make them do something. And they appreciate it always.
Back to Australia, what about Keith Hounslow's band, how do you pronounce that?

Hounslow, that's right. He was a West Australian who came over to Melbourne purely and simply because jazz was happening in Melbourne. And he came over playing early Armstrong type of stuff. He was playing some beautiful music. He was young, keen. Gradually he changed. He's now playing the most far out modern jazz that anyone is playing in Australia. But he's playing hot modern jazz, which is good. And he's still prepared to have a go at things, even if he makes a mistake or two. He's one of the reasons why I, without knowing anything about modern jazz, I don't sort of laugh at it or discard it at all. Obviously, there are chaps who really believe in it and sincerely try to play in that style. It's a different sort of music to my mind. But that's what happened to Keith.
And is there much modern jazz over there? Is that a big competition? Not very much.
No, no, there's not much.
They had that Australian jazz quartet which came to this country. They're not very well known in Australia.
Yeah.
What about Ken Owens' band? What was that?

Ken Owens, he was a boy wonder, 16, 17 years old. He was playing beautiful sounding stuff on cornet. He just never developed, unfortunately. He's still occasionally playing very promising sort of stuff, but not, he's just never developed. He's now, he must be in his mid-thirties. He's just never made it. He's around your age, huh? Yes, yes. He, I just can't understand it.
And Ian Burns, is he the one that's playing yet?

No, he, unfortunately, he was a fine pianist, strong sort of honky-tonk sort of style. And, unfortunately, he died suddenly, something caught in his throat or something. Oh. Yes, it was very, he was playing with the Frank Johnson band. And, suddenly, we heard he died at a big funeral for him. We played at the funeral.
The band, didn't it? Yes, Flea's a Bird and all that. At the grave side? Yes, at the grave side.

We didn't want to, or we sort of didn't want to if it was going to affect his relatives at all. You know, they didn't know anything about jazz. But, his wife insisted. Mm-hmm. So, we did it. They were very happy about it. Happy. They were very glad we did it. Mm-hmm.
And what about John's sewing stuff?

He was the chap I used to play with most of all before I joined the Johnson band. Mm-hmm. He is a very keen cornet player. But, he was rough. He was pretty awful for a while. I can remember playing with him and thinking, oh, gosh, this is no value at all. He's so far off. He's sort of very keen, but he just can't get it. Suddenly, it all came. Obviously, he'd been practicing and thinking about it, but these things take time. Suddenly, it all sort of came to his fingertips and the 1948 Jazz Convention, he suddenly surprised everyone by playing a wonderful driving sort of cornet. No particular style. Mm-hmm. It was just tremendous stuff. He didn't keep it up for long and then he joined the Graham Bell Band as drummer on their second tour. Mm-hmm. He got into modern playing then and he's been on that since. Modern drummer now? Yes, and cornet. Mm-hmm. He was the one who killed his mother with an axe because she wouldn't let him go to a Graham Bell concert, which made things quite worrying sometimes. I can't believe that. Are you making that up? No, this sounds like an early New Orleans legend, I know. No, he did this, but he was so young they sort of let him off. And let him off. Sometimes I used to think I'd better not make any mistakes when playing with him. Yeah. But there was no sign of that in him really, except that he was terribly enthusiastic.
What about Kit Orrie's band and what Kerry and those people, did they have any influence out there? Well, yes, they had a great influence on me.

I heard very early in the piece, I heard Kit Orrie band with Donald Howard, a session they made there, and I don't know why, I've heard Donald Howard several times since on record and he hasn't been impressive at all. On that particular record he was very impressive. I was particularly struck by it. In fact, I would say that probably, now I'm thinking of the answers to much earlier questions, Rod Kless with the Maxi Spania band was a strong influence on me because the Spania records were just coming out, I'd rush into the stores and get the new one that had come out each three months, they'd bring out a new one. Of that session, the 38 session, but they were coming out about 40, 41 in Australia.
And high school then, what we call high school.

Yes. Yes, I would have been. Rod Kless and then this Orrie session with Donald Howard, very free flowing sort of stuff, that had a great effect on me, yes. So that, but by and large I don't suppose the Orrie band did have any sort of great effect on any number of musicians.
Yeah, except maybe through Ken Collier, I feel that Mutt influenced him.

Collier, yes, I've always thought this, no one seems to say this very much, but I've always thought that he's a real Mutt type player. Well we talked about that, he and I, you know. Did he think that himself?

Oh yeah, yeah, and he would discuss how Mutt would change his whole phrasing and tone from one chorus to another. Yes, yes. And change the whole sound of the band. Yes, yes, yes. What about your own repertoire of tunes that you feature on clarinet?

Ah yes, well of course I don't like feature melodies and things, but we found out very very soon, very quickly when we went to England, we were playing sessions every night, that the brass men just couldn't keep up with it, lips would be shattered and so on, so that I'd have to do some numbers occasionally and it wasn't too bad because it gave me an opportunity to feature things that I used to play around with at home a bit. I like getting onto rags and piano rags and playing them on clarinet and trying to play them fairly authentically, get all the sort of phrases and things in as much as a single melody line can do it. But, and then to use them as a vehicle for improvising in the last few choruses. So I was doing quite a bit of that sort of stuff in the last couple of years and I've had great fun playing things like Perfect Rag, Nonsense Rag, quite a few of the Tony Parenti ones. In fact one that he wrote, Crawfish Crawl, things like that. It's, I've had quite fun playing those. They're different again. I play less like Lewis then. Somewhere I'll find a style that's mine eventually I suppose.
What's strange do you use when you, you hear me, improvise?
I don't, I don't have any set rule. I just try to find the, the part that seems to sit first. I suppose it's generally the trio because it generally sits first, but not all those.
On Perfect Rag?
Perfect Rag I know that I go back to the first part. Although, the fact is that I do improvise on the trio a little bit before I go back to the first part.
And you modulate back to the original key.
Yes, yes, modulate back to the original one. Instead of doing that.
Now, you can, do you listen to the record of Perfect Rag or do you look at the sheet music of it or?
No, I do it off the record. I always have. From the record.

I got it from the old Jolly 1923 Genet I think, recording of Perfect Drag. I think that was it. I just played it over and over and over and over again until I got a melody out of it and got some idea of the chords. What I have done each year at the jazz conventions for quite a few years, I've teamed up with a very fine pianist, probably our best pianist in Australia, Graham Coyle. We've played, we had what we call the Polites Coyle Ragtimers, just as a name of a group, playing only at the jazz convention. And it's become a bit of an institution at the jazz conventions. We play all these rag-type tunes.
I wondered about who some of your favorite musicians were, just in general, any instrument or any approach to jazz. Not necessarily jazz, that's what you like.

Well, it's jazz. I listen to jazz, I suppose, only. It just doesn't seem to be time to listen to jazz enough, much less to other things. I can't, I'm not, not sort of, madly interested in solo work as such, so that I listen more for ensemble and try and play that in the band. And, undoubtedly, Lewis must feature strongly in it. Although I see quite a lot of fault in his playing and all this sort of thing. He's got the great sort of commanding glory that he plays hot. That's the thing that counts. Dodds, I still very much enjoy listening to Dodds all the time, even though I don't attempt to play that much in his style. Although, the Dodds that played with King Oliver is a fine style, which I probably do try to play a bit like, because that's just about a perfect New Orleans ensemble style, I think. Well, then there's, I'm assuming, with the Jelly Roll, Morton, and things. I like jazz, you know, generally. It's hard to.
It's hard to pick out one. I think we're just about running out of.
So we might as well call it to a halt.
